description:
ICL students focused on developing AI interface for microgravity thermal safety analysis for engineers, providing safe and validated bounds for engineering design in a range of environments. 

Team member Diciplines:

Aeronautical Engineering x2

Electronic and Information Engineering x2

Electrical and Electronic Engineering x1

Physics x1
summary: The IC Dynamics Dashboard (ICDD) provides engineers, students and researchers with a SI-powered personal thermodynamics consultant for first approximation of combustion properties in user specified environments. The ICDD accelerates the design decision stage for engineers, literature review for researchers, and provides concise topic exploration for students through SI abstraction of user input and application of validated scientific models. Our dashboard holds the potential to be transformative to the thermodynamic design and research disciplines, enabling quick and easy access to a pool of SI interpreted NASA data.
details:
The overarching scope is as follows: user input is taken in the form of text regarding a relevant query, pending design decision, or general search. The dashboard translates this input into SI-abstracted parameters, through which relevant NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets are fetched and fed into pre-developed thermodynamic and heat transfer models grounded in validated combustion theory. Model outputs are then interpreted and passed back to the SI layer, which formats and presents actionable results, regime classifications, and visual diagnostics on the web-based dashboard, referencing and redirecting to the dataset as appropriate.

The thermodynamics team developed 20 modular python solvers spanning gas-phase chemical equilibrium, boundary-layer flame spread, multiphase droplet combustion, radiative quenching, and habitat control-volume dynamics. These routines solve First Law enthalpy balances, Gibbs free energy minimization, Chapman-Enskog transport properties, and dimensionless scaling groups (Da, Le, Ri and Spalding B numbers). Coupling these models with NASA PSI telemetry, including BASS-II, SAFFIRE, FLEX, ACME, and SAME, the dashboard reduces combustion problems into quantitative fire-safety margins and theoretical partial-gravity bounds for spacecraft, Lunar, and Martian habitats, with potential for on-Earth application based on user intent. Applications include screening spacecraft materials against Earth 1g standards (NASA-STD-6001) via microgravity Limiting Oxygen Index LOI (0g) defining safe cabin ventilation envelopes between low-flow radiative quenching and convective blow-off, sizing inert suppressants (CO2, He, CO2 and fine water mist), predicting closed-cabin pressure and toxicity transients, and guiding smoke detector selection, alongside terrestrial extensions such as fire-retardant textile evaluation and mist suppression. By turning experimental archives into interpretable and actional output, the project helps engineers assess fire risks in reduced-pressure, oxygen-enriched exploration atmospheres (such as proposed 10.2 PSI / 30% O2Lunar habitats) while making microgravity fire physics intuitive for researchers and students.

The solvers were built in Python (using SciPy, and analytical kinetic-theory), linked to the web dashboard through standardized JSON input/output contracts and version-controlled via GitHub. The larger thermodynamic models were SI-produced, with iterative steering and verification based on our own theoretical understanding of the subject to ensure precise programs. This architecture evidences the project's innovation: not asking an SI model to guess values (risking hallucination), we use SI for natural-language semantic routing and interpretation while delegating all calculations to validated conservation laws, adapting output depth and 1g vs. 0gvisual comparisons for a range of user roles.

Throughout development, our team considered several critical engineering and scientific guardrails. Because NASA PSI currently contains no direct Lunar (0.16g) or Martian (0.38g) combustion data, every partial-gravity output is explicitly labelled as a theoretical bound rather than an empirical flight measurement. We also structured model routing to preserve hardware and scale distinctions across NASA experiments, while accounting for counterintuitive microgravity hazards such as invisible cool-flame reignition and materials that pass 1g upward-burn screening yet remain flammable in low-speed 0g airflow.

On the data and orchestration side, the AI team built a knowledge graph indexing 19 microgravity combustion investigations, 2,038 experiment records, and more than 61,000 supporting resources, including raw measurement CSVs, test videos, and Final Science Reports. When a query is submitted, a hybrid retrieval engine combines lexical search, domain concept filtering, and vector similarity to rank relevant runs without cross-contaminating distinct experimental campaigns. The SI orchestrator acts as a schema-constrained planner that runs up to three bounded inspection rounds in a temporary sandbox, downloading candidate files to verify exact column headers, data types, and physical units before mapping them into solver inputs via explicit JSON pointers. If required variables or units remain unverified, the pipeline fails fast as opposed to guessing conversions.

To build this embedding-based parser, we used a closed-loop hierarchical agentic workflow. Autonomous agents first generated a contextualized test dataset designed to replicate how humans naturally phrase queries, which we combined with additional prompts written by aerospace engineers to establish an evaluation set. Agents scored the parser against a structured rubric measuring retrieval and extraction accuracy and execution time, passing identified failure modes back to a manager agent. The manager agent then dispatched parallel updates iteratively until the pipeline hit full accuracy, and satisfied the simplicity rubric, followed by a final review with a human engineer.

Once a validated execution plan is assembled, the selected physics routines execute inside isolated worker subprocesses with bounded CPU and memory limits. Each worker returns numerical results alongside interactive chart coordinate series, recorded experimental caveats, and direct links to the cited NASA reports and flight videos, giving engineers and researchers end-to-end traceability from raw telemetry to calculated safety margins.

On the front end, we created a dedicated Markdown design specification containing clear layout rules with an explicit list of UI failure modes to ensure the dashboard remained simple to navigate and thematically relevant. We started by using SI to generate 20 initial design concepts, shortlisting the stronger candidates while updating our Markdown ruleset with both newly identified failure conditions and specific interface elements we wanted to keep. Through structured iteration against those constraints, we refined the design models until landing on the final layout.

Overall, our program holds immense potential to transform the thermodynamic sector workflow as a personalized consultant and assistant for engineering design decisions across a range of environments, generating bounding safety margins based on NASA data. Moreover, researchers may find use in reapplying much of the information to ongoing thermodynamic research on combustion on earth, using the 1g environment, or extrapolate to Martian or Lunar research. Similarly, the dashboard offers a creative outlet for students to engage with and identify research gaps in contemporary combustion and fire safety research, as well as informing their own future endeavours within the field.
